node.label: Alfred W. Crosby
node.date_label: The Columbian Exchange 1972 · Virgin Soil Epidemics 1976 · Ecological Imperialism 1986
node.description: A historian of the biological consequences of European expansion. The Columbian Exchange (1972) followed pathogens, plants and animals between the Americas and the Old World after 1492, and 'Virgin Soil Epidemics' (1976) defined epidemics among peoples who, as Jones (2003, pp. 703–704) quotes the definition, 'have had no previous contact with the diseases that strike them' (the 1976 article itself is unread). Ecological Imperialism (1986) starts from the fact that 'European emigrants and their descendants are all over the place, which requires explanation', asks why 'the sun never sets on the empire of the dandelion', and suggests that 'the success of European imperialism has a biological, an ecological, component': crops, livestock, weeds and diseases helped Europeans make temperate 'Neo-Europes'. Later critics charge the model with ecological determinism and argue that the virgin-soil idea was flattened into a claim that Indigenous Americans had 'no immunity'.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Alfred W. Crosby (1931–2018); The Columbian Exchange: Biological and Cultural Consequences of 1492 (1972); 'Virgin Soil Epidemics as a Factor in the Aboriginal Depopulation in America' (William and Mary Quarterly, 1976); Ecological Imperialism: The Biological Expansion of Europe, 900–1900 (1986); 'The Past and Present of Environmental History' (American Historical Review, 1995). Readings: Miller's review (1987); Cook (1990); Cronon (1993); Subrahmanyam (1997); later, Jones (2003), McNeill (2003) and Isenberg (2013).
node.scope_note: This entry presents Ecological Imperialism as its prologue states the argument (pp. 1–7 read, with the contents and acknowledgments, in the publisher's sample of the 2004 second edition; page numbers are that edition's). The Columbian Exchange (1972), 'Virgin Soil Epidemics' (1976) and the 1995 AHR essay are unread: the 1972 book is characterised from Cook (1990) and McNeill (2003), and the 1976 wording is quoted as Jones (2003) quotes it. His 1978 American Heritage essay on New England, read in full, states the disease argument in his own words: 'Innocent of immunity or experience, the Indians were helpless.' He is not presented as the founder of environmental history: the ASEH's own history lists him among several 'founding members' with Worster, Flader and Opie, and in 1982 among 'the already widely known historians'; he thanks William McNeill, who 'read the whole thing in first draft'. Contested readings: in period, Subrahmanyam (1997) calls the books 'oft-cited (and oft-criticized)', while Miller (1987) finds Crosby 'careful not to overestimate the significance of any single component'. Later, McNeill (2003) records that 'Some readers felt that Crosby had relocated historical agency (and responsibility for genocide and colonialism) from humans to wheat and whooping cough'; Isenberg (2013) judges that his analysis 'devolved into little more than ecological determinism'; Jones (2003) argues that the virgin-soil model 'has been misunderstood and misrepresented', that the 1976 article itself stressed malnutrition and 'the social chaos generated by European colonization', and that Crosby's other writings stressed lack of immunity. These are later readings, not evidence for the edges. The 2004 preface, in which he calls Pomeranz's Great Divergence 'The clearest exposition of the new scenario', is a later self-reading and is not used.

incident_edges.relationship: Introduced organisms and pathogens as causes in colonial history: the Columbian exchange (1972) and ecological imperialism (1986)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Crosby's own statement, Ecological Imperialism (1986), prologue (pp. 1–7 read; 2004-edition pagination). It opens: 'European emigrants and their descendants are all over the place, which requires explanation' (p. 2), and names 'what I shall call the Neo-Europes' (p. 2). Underlying the pull of these lands 'were factors perhaps best described as biogeographical' (p. 5). 'European flora and fauna, including human beings, can thrive in these regions if the competition is not too fierce'; 'Perhaps European humans have triumphed because of their superiority in arms, organization, and fanaticism, but what in heaven's name is the reason that the sun never sets on the empire of the dandelion? Perhaps the success of European imperialism has a biological, an ecological, component' (p. 7). The contents give chapters 'Weeds' (145), 'Animals' (171) and 'Ills' (195). His 1978 American Heritage essay on Plymouth (web text read in full; no print pages) makes the disease argument for New England: 'Disease was among the commodities, and in this trade the Indians would come off second best'; 'Innocent of immunity or experience, the Indians were helpless'; the Pilgrims survived 'thanks more to biology than religion'. In-period reception inside the field: Cronon's 1993 ASEH address (read) turns the two books into lessons of environmental history, 'When people migrate from one ecosystem to another, they carry with them other organisms—plants, animals, microbes—whose success or failure in the new location is often crucial in determining the success or failure of the migration' (p. 8) and 'Beware of bugs that come from afar' (p. 10), both footnoted to The Columbian Exchange and Ecological Imperialism (nn. 16, 25, p. 22). Cook's 1990 essay, read, takes The Columbian Exchange as the model for an ecological reading of Canadian contact: 'As Alfred W. Crosbie [sic], Jr., demonstrated so brilliantly nearly two decades ago ... contact was even more significantly the interaction of different ecologies or environments' (p. 13, n. 35). Miller's 1987 review (Medical History, read in full) calls the book 'a vividly written account of ecological transition' and finds Crosby 'careful not to overestimate the significance of any single component' (p. 374). The ASEH's history page (undated institutional account, read) records him commenting on the keynote at the society's first conference (Irvine, 1982) and lists him among 'founding members of our society such as Don Worster, Susan Flader, Alfred Crosby, and Opie himself'. A contribution, not a founding: no text read calls him the founder. Melville's adaptation of his question to Mexico (1994) is recorded in the existing melville_plague note, not rechecked. McNeill (2003, pp. 24, 33) and Isenberg (2013, p. 86), with their criticism of determinism, are later readings, not evidence for this edge.

incident_edges.relationship: Ecological change at world scale: the biological expansion of Europe and the making of Neo-Europes, 900–1900 (1986)
incident_edges.evidence_note: The scale and question of Ecological Imperialism (1986), prologue and contents (read; 2004-edition pagination). Other peoples expanded into adjacent lands, but 'Europeans, in contrast, seem to have leapfrogged around the globe' to Neo-Europes, 'lands thousands of kilometers from Europe and from each other' (p. 2); the book runs from 'The Norse and the Crusaders' and 'The Fortunate Isles' through 'Winds' to 'New Zealand' (contents, pp. xi–xii), and asks whether 'the success of European imperialism has a biological, an ecological, component' (p. 7). He thanks 'William McNeill, who read the whole thing in first draft' (acknowledgments, p. xxii); McNeill is the world-history synthesiser on the global entry. In-period uptake by connected history: Subrahmanyam (1997, p. 738, re-read) lists among early modern shifts 'travel, discovery and colonization as leading to an ecological shift of global dimensions', and his note 10 points to 'the oft-cited (and oft-criticized) works of Alfred Crosby (The Columbian Exchange, and Ecological Imperialism)', adding that Grove's Green Imperialism 'pays far greater attention to Asia than does Crosby'. A contribution, not a founding, and a resource with stated limits: Subrahmanyam's own note marks it as criticised and as giving Asia less attention than Grove. Later readings, not evidence for this edge: McNeill (2003, p. 32) calls it 'Perhaps the best-known among the thematically defined global-scale environmental histories'; Crosby's 2004 preface names Pomeranz's Great Divergence 'The clearest exposition of the new scenario' and says 'I am proud to have contributed to it' (pp. xvii, xx).

neighbor_nodes.label: Environmental history
neighbor_nodes.date_label: 1970s consolidation · Environmental History (journal) 1996 · NiCHE 2004 · Canadian number of Environmental History 2007 · Sutter forum 2013 · Oxford Handbook 2014 · reviewed through 2024
neighbor_nodes.description: Explains historical relations among people and the nonhuman world through ecological exchange, agriculture, property, commodity flows, conservation and cultural ideas of nature; the approaches disagree about causal emphasis, and cases from New England, the Great Plains, Mexico, India, colonial islands and South Africa connect ecology with power without one model. Bullard and the Huggins life histories add unequal burdens and authority over accounts; the Dust Bowl debates set capitalism, technology, policy and survival against one another. After 1995 the field argued with itself and its neighbours: Cronon called wilderness 'quite profoundly a human creation'; Foreman answered that this 'Received Wilderness Idea is a straw dog; it does not exist on the ground' (2000); Spence (1999) examined Indian removal in the making of national parks. A merged journal (1996), McNeill's world synthesis (2000) and a Canadian network (NiCHE, 2004) widened it; by 2013 Sutter found nature and culture replaced by 'environmental hybridity' (editors' summary). Chakrabarty (2009) and the Anthropocene histories of 2016 set its questions at planetary scale.
neighbor_nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Alfred Crosby; Donald Worster; Carolyn Merchant; William Cronon. ASEH founded 1977. Expanded contextual readings include Leopold’s precursor essays, Melville’s Mexican study, Gadgil and Guha’s Indian history, Grove’s colonial conservation and Carruthers’s South African park history. After 2000: J. R. McNeill, Something New Under the Sun (2000) and 'Observations' (2003); Spence, Dispossessing the Wilderness (1999); Jacoby, Crimes against Nature (2001); Sutter, 'The World with Us' (JAH 2013); Isenberg, ed., The Oxford Handbook of Environmental History (2014); in Canada, Wynn (series editor), MacEachern, Loo, Piper, Sandlos, Evenden, Colpitts, Parr; the Anthropocene: Chakrabarty (2009), McNeill and Engelke, Malm, Bonneuil and Fressoz (2016). Institutions: Environmental History (journal, 1996), NiCHE (2004).

neighbor_nodes.scope_note: Ecological exchange, political economy, and feminist critiques of nature overlap; institutional society history does not document every intellectual route. Crosby’s temperate-settler argument differs from Melville’s Mexican case; Gadgil and Guha’s resource conflicts differ from Grove’s conservation networks and Carruthers’s park politics. Cronon’s cultural account of wilderness does not deny nonhuman nature. The selection remains incomplete, especially in environmental justice and Indigenous scholarship. A bounded second-pass addition now compares Bullard and the Huggins collaboration; primary-excerpt, publisher-description and metadata limits remain distinct, and neither selection represents every community. Extended to 2024 on 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md). Read in full: Foreman's 'The Real Wilderness Idea' (2000), Cronon's CV and 'The Riddle of the Apostle Islands' (2003), the NiCHE and UBC Press series pages, publisher pages and abstracts for the Canadian books and articles, two open reviews of Worster's Shrinking the Earth; passages read: Cronon's 'Storytelling' (2013) and McNeill's AHA address (2020). Unread: the 1996 comments by Hays, Cohen and Dunlap and Cronon's response; Sutter's 2013 essay and its six responses (the editors' summary is quoted instead); McNeill 2000 and 2003 (the latter known from the earlier record); the 2005 'What's Next' forum including Linda Nash on agency; the bodies of every Canadian book; Malm, Moore, Bonneuil and Fressoz beyond descriptions. The History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23 dates the field's readership: 1.6% of Canada + US theses cited two or more of its authors in the 1990s, 5.7% in 2000–09, 9.5% in 2010–14, 11.3% in 2015–19, 9.9% in 2020–25; the network of works co-cited with its founders (Cronon's Changes, Nature's Metropolis and 'The Trouble with Wilderness'; Worster's Dust Bowl, Rivers of Empire and Nature's Economy; White's Organic Machine; Crosby's Ecological Imperialism; Merchant's Death of Nature; works with lift ≥ 3, averaged over repeated samples of fifteen seed-citing theses) peaked in Canada in 2010–14 (37 works) and halved by 2020–25 (17), its new members being Wolfe and Tuck and Yang; in the US it is stable (17–19 works) and its entrants are Indigenous, borderlands and slavery works. The History PhD citation graph interprets these sampled co-citation neighbourhoods as diffusion into neighbouring historiographies. This does not establish declining scholarly production or the field's own understanding of its development.

strands.focus: Changing resource-use systems, state interventions and resistance connect ecological and social histories without making precolonial society uniformly harmonious.
strands.works: This Fissured Land (1992)

strands.title: Conservation, colonial science and racial power
strands.focus: Grove studies colonial conservation networks and islands; Carruthers studies a South African park’s racial and national politics. These distinct scales complicate a purely benevolent conservation story.
strands.works: Green Imperialism (1995); The Kruger National Park (1995)

strands.title: Wilderness as a historical cultural idea
strands.focus: Cronon examines the pristine-wilderness ideal and Indigenous removal, while defending care for nonhuman nature in inhabited places.
strands.works: “The Trouble with Wilderness” (1995; journal reprint with comments and a response, Environmental History 1:1, January 1996)

strands.title: Historical geography in environmental-history teaching
strands.focus: Cronon’s 1994 syllabus assigns Sauer’s 1941 essay among several resources for bringing nature into history. Assignment demonstrates use without establishing assent or an exclusive intellectual ancestry.
strands.works: History 901 syllabus (Fall 1994), 14 September readings

strands.title: Unequal pollution burdens and collective action
strands.focus: Bullard joins environmental distribution with race, class and organizing capacity. The Alsen case distinguishes partial gains from unresolved health concerns and internal disagreement.
strands.works: Dumping in Dixie (1990), selected reprinted excerpts

strands.title: Country, displacement and historical voice
strands.focus: Read Rita and Jackie Huggins’s situated life-history project beside conservation and settler-landscape narratives. Publisher descriptions support this bounded comparison; their full books and place article remain unread.
strands.works: Auntie Rita (1994); Changes in the Land (1983); The Kruger National Park (1995)

strands.title: Agricultural culture, technology and regional causes
strands.focus: Worster argues for interacting natural and cultural forces while emphasizing agricultural capitalism. McDean criticizes his generalization, contests Bonnifield’s federal-policy account and favors Hurt’s regional specificity. These are competing interpretations.
strands.works: Worster (1986); McDean (1986), discussing books of 1979 and 1981

strands.title: Ecological adaptation and the promise of development
strands.focus: Worster acknowledges Malin’s ecological history but disputes explanations through natural storms and a passing pioneering stage. He distinguishes rival cultural values and varied regional entrepreneurial intensity.
strands.works: Malin (1946,1950), critically discussed by Worster (1986)

strands.title: Regional boundaries and histories of staying
strands.focus: Compare McDean’s insistence on a specific Dust Bowl region, Fite’s call for northern Plains coverage, and Riney-Kehrberg’s household survival study in southwestern Kansas. Causal explanation, geographical scale and lived experience pose different questions.
strands.works: McDean (1986); Fite (1983); Rooted in Dust (1994)

strands.title: Wilderness, livelihood and different political contexts
strands.focus: Guha targets American deep ecology’s universal claims and conservation’s unequal costs in India, while acknowledging Naess’s concern about inequality. Cronon studies American sublime/frontier ideals and everyday responsibility, explicitly citing Guha in note28. Shared concerns about exclusion do not erase their different contexts or Cronon’s support for protected wild lands.
strands.works: Guha (1989); Cronon (1995), including note28

strands.title: Can biocentrism incorporate social criticism?
strands.focus: Johns’s abstract disputes Guha’s equation of deep ecology with wilderness protection and defends biocentrism joined to critical social theory against overconsumption and militarism. This is a named response; the article’s detailed reasoning is not newly verified.
strands.works: Guha (1989); Johns (1990), abstract

strands.title: Cultural criticism and habitat protection
strands.focus: Sessions objects that Cronon underweights biodiversity and connected wild habitat. His claim that cultural construction conflicts with independent nature is a critical interpretation: Cronon explicitly defends nonhuman autonomy and wild-land protection.
strands.works: Cronon (1995); Sessions (1996)

strands.title: Material change, ideas and gendered nature
strands.focus: Merchant retrospectively clarifies that ecological and economic changes made some ideas more plausible rather than mechanically causing them. Her socialist ecofeminism addresses production and reproduction and challenges an essentialist identification of women with nature.
strands.works: The Death of Nature (1980); Radical Ecology (1992), discussed in Merchant’s 2006 retrospective

strands.title: Colonial conservation: knowledge, power and benefits
strands.focus: Carruthers’s review welcomes Grove’s island settings and exchanges of knowledge, while questioning parts of his synthesis. Her Kruger prologue and epilogue emphasize changing political coalitions, racial exclusion and allocation of benefits. Scientific conservation and unequal power can coexist; these works ask different questions at different scales.
strands.works: Green Imperialism (1995), reviewed by Carruthers (1996); The Kruger National Park (1995), prologue and epilogue

strands.title: The wilderness debate, 1995–2000: a selected exchange
strands.focus: Cronon's essay (1995; reprinted with comments in the first number of Environmental History, January 1996) held wilderness to be 'quite profoundly a human creation' and 'a flight from history' while defending wild-land protection. Hays replied in the journal that 'Cronon's wilderness is a world of abstracted ideas … divorced from the values and ideas inherent in wilderness action' (as quoted by Foreman; comment unread). Sessions objected from conservation biology (1996). Callicott and Nelson gathered thirty-nine essays as The Great New Wilderness Debate (1998), where Foreman's 'Wilderness Areas for Real' answered. Foreman then told a federal wilderness-science conference (1999; printed 2000) that he came 'not to praise The Received Wilderness Idea, but to bury it': the idea that 'Baird Callicott, Bill Cronon and other postmodern deconstructionist scholars so eagerly banish' was 'a straw dog; it does not exist on the ground', unlike 'the Real Wilderness Idea' that built the National Wilderness Preservation System. A selected exchange: Cohen's and Dunlap's comments, the editors' introduction to the anthology and Cronon's 1996 response (pp. 47–55) are unread; in 2003 he answered in practice, asking that the Apostle Islands be managed 'as a historical wilderness' — 'Emphatically yes' to designation, but 'a storied wilderness'.
strands.works: 'The Trouble with Wilderness' (1995; Environmental History 1:1, 1996, with comments and a response); Callicott and Nelson, eds., The Great New Wilderness Debate (1998); Foreman, 'The Real Wilderness Idea' (2000); Cronon, 'The Riddle of the Apostle Islands' (2003)

strands.title: The Anthropocene and the climate of history
strands.focus: Chakrabarty's four theses (2009) held that anthropogenic climate change collapses the distinction between natural and human history (edge_918; critics at edge_1147). Environmental historians then wrote the epoch: McNeill and Engelke's The Great Acceleration (2016) says 'The Earth has entered a new age—the Anthropocene' and that 'human dependence on fossil fuels inaugurated' it; Malm's Fossil Capital (2016) answers that 'steam offered neither cheaper nor more abundant energy' but control over labour, against what a reviewer on its cover calls the 'Anthropocene narrative'; Bonneuil and Fressoz refuse 'the convenient view of a "human species" that upset the Earth system, unaware of what it was doing' (publisher descriptions; bodies unread). Worster's Shrinking the Earth (2016) was read by Collomb as 'reflections of the greatest US environmental historian on humankind's future and the Anthropocene'. McNeill told the AHA (2020) that 'environmental history stands to be disrupted, and with luck enhanced, more than most fields'. In PhD bibliographies this is a strand of the historiography, not of reading: Chakrabarty is cited by 4.5% of Canada + US theses in 2020–25, in three families (History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23).
strands.works: Chakrabarty, 'The Climate of History' (2009); McNeill and Engelke, The Great Acceleration (2016); Malm, Fossil Capital (2016); Bonneuil and Fressoz, The Shock of the Anthropocene (2016); Worster, Shrinking the Earth (2016)

strands.title: Canadian environmental history: a network and a series, 2001–2019
strands.focus: Wynn (2003) found the field 'undeveloped in this country, compared with the United States'. Within a decade it had institutions: NiCHE, 'founded in fall 2004 by a small team of scholars' and funded by a SSHRC Strategic Knowledge Cluster grant from 2007 (MacEachern director; Wynn, Turkel, Castonguay, Evenden and Piper on the executive); Wynn's UBC Press series Nature | History | Society, 'devoted to the publication of high-quality scholarship in environmental history and allied fields'; and a Canadian number of Environmental History (October 2007, edited by Evenden and MacEachern) in which Piper and Sandlos found that 'the Canadian North was never subject to the broad ecological transformation that occurred further to the south' and Loo argued that environmental justice 'requires coming to terms with the different scales' at which change is apprehended. The books — MacEachern on Atlantic parks (2001), Evenden on the Fraser (2004), Loo on wildlife (2006), Sandlos on northern game laws (2007), Piper on subarctic industry (2009), Parr on the senses (2010), Colpitts on pemmican (2014), Loo on relocation (2019) — won the CHA's prizes and, in Canadian PhD bibliographies, entered the company of Cronon, Worster and White in 2010–19 (MacEachern and Loo in 2010–14; Parr, Piper, Evenden and Sandlos in 2015–19; History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23). Loo (2014) asked the field to 'use more of the world, and vice versa'.
strands.works: NiCHE (2004); Nature | History | Society (UBC Press); Environmental History 12:4 (2007); MacEachern (2001), Evenden (2004), Loo (2006, 2019), Sandlos (2007), Piper (2009), Parr (2010), Colpitts (2014); Loo, 'Missed Connections' (2014)

strands.title: Conservation, dispossession and neighbouring historiographies
strands.focus: Cronon wrote that 'The removal of Indians to create an "uninhabited wilderness"' showed 'just how invented, just how constructed, the American wilderness really is' (1995). Spence (1999) examined Indian removal in the making of national parks: Dispossessing the Wilderness traced how 'the early conception of the wilderness as the place where Indians lived (or should live)' gave way to 'the idealization of uninhabited wilderness' at Yellowstone, Glacier and Yosemite. Warren's The Hunter's Game (1997) and Jacoby's Crimes against Nature (2001; Marsh and Littleton-Griswold prizes), by Cronon's doctoral students, wrote the social history of poaching and conservation (unread; no reader read here links them to the wilderness essay). In Canada, Binnema and Niemi (2006) argued that the Stoney were excluded from Banff for game conservation, sport hunting, tourism and assimilation rather than for a wilderness ideal, and Sandlos (2007) that game laws and sanctuaries 'helped the state assert authority over traditional hunting cultures'; Daschuk's Clearing the Plains (2013), with disease and climate among its causes, is blurbed by McNeill and read with Wolfe. The dissertation record records an associated readership pattern: the works newly co-cited with the field's founders after 2015 are Wolfe, Tuck and Yang, The Middle Ground, Hämäläinen, DuVal and O'Brien (History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23; founders Cronon ×3, Worster ×3, White, Crosby, Merchant; lift ≥ 3; averaged over repeated samples of fifteen seed-citing theses). Settler colonial studies is its own entry; the link between the two is drawn there.
strands.works: Warren, The Hunter's Game (1997); Spence, Dispossessing the Wilderness (1999); Jacoby, Crimes against Nature (2001); Binnema and Niemi (2006); Sandlos, Hunters at the Margin (2007); Daschuk, Clearing the Plains (2013)

coverage.basis: Reviewed through 2000 in the original 1920–2000 experiment; extended to 2024 on 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md) on the wilderness debate (Foreman 2000 read in full; the 1996 journal comments unread), the field's surveys (McNeill 2003 from the earlier record; Sutter 2013 by the editors' summary and abstract; Isenberg 2014 by abstract and contents), the Canadian field (NiCHE and UBC Press pages, publisher pages and abstracts 2001–2019) and the Anthropocene histories (publisher descriptions). The History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23 gives the readership: 5.7% of Canada + US theses cited two or more of the field's authors in 2000–09, 9.5% in 2010–14, 11.3% in 2015–19, 9.9% in 2020–25 (Canada 10.2%, US 9.7%); the works co-cited with nine founding titles by Cronon, Worster, White, Crosby and Merchant (lift ≥ 3, averaged over repeated samples of fifteen seed-citing theses) peaked in Canada in 2010–14 and halved by 2020–25, the new members being Wolfe and Tuck and Yang; the US network is stable in size, its entrants Indigenous, borderlands and slavery works. The citation graph interprets these neighbourhoods as diffusion into neighbouring historiographies; this does not establish declining scholarly production or the field's own understanding of its development. The later texts named here are dated individually; the bodies of most are unread.
